Men of Zhang Xiaolin's stamp were bred only by that age and that setting—which is to say, by the Shanghai concessions around the nineteen-twenties.
Without the concessions, such men would never have arisen at all; and so one may say that the foreign concessions on Chinese soil were the very cradle of the breed.

Men of this kind represented the latent forces of a deformed society—not necessarily evil forces, the line between them lying in whether a man inclined toward good or toward evil. In native disposition alone, good and evil in them did not stand in any fixed proportion.

Their sphere of power was confined, in the main, to the concessions, though at times it reached beyond them; yet the farther one went from the concessions, the weaker that influence grew, until it faded away altogether. Looked at from another angle, some of those outside the concessions had nonetheless to earn their bread by way of the concessions, and so dared not give these men offense.
Such leading figures, then, ought surely to have a name; and indeed they were commonly called the “Shanghai tycoons.” To be more exact, I think “concession tycoons” the apter term.

Note well that the “concession tycoon” of Shanghai was a thing distinct from the imported “underworld boss.” The underworld boss made his trade of villainy and crime, with an eye to profit and profit alone; the concession tycoon was a man who had already arrived, who had learned to guard his good name, and who wanted, besides profit, reputation as well—so that in his conduct he was forever wishing to “wash his hands in the golden basin” and strive toward respectability. Whether he ever washed both hands quite clean, however, was another matter.

Today the “concessions” have become a term of history; but in their day they wrought no small effect upon our country's politics and economy, and in the matter of social manners they did our people's morals a deep and lasting injury. The writer is none too well versed in the question of the concessions, and so, drawing upon the introductory portion of The Question of the Shanghai Concessions, published by the Zhengzhong Book Company, sets it out as follows:

“The Shanghai concessions comprised the International Settlement and the French Concession. By the Sino-British Treaty of Nanjing, concluded in the twenty-second year of the Qing Daoguang reign (1842), the British were permitted to reside and trade at Shanghai. The next year the first British consul at Shanghai, Balfour, reached his post; before long the opening of Shanghai to trade was proclaimed, and he marked out the bounds of the concession together with the Shanghai daotai Gong Mujiu—and this was the British concession at Shanghai.

“Through the contrivance of the American Bishop Boone, an American settlement had in fact existed since the twenty-eighth year of Daoguang (1848) along the Hongkou district on the left bank of Suzhou Creek. This had been a desolate quarter, with few inhabitants; but after Liu Lichuan's ‘Small Swords’ and the Hong-Yang ‘Taiping’ rebellion, its importance suddenly grew. In the third year of the Qing Tongzhi reign (1864) the Shanghai daotai and the American consul at Shanghai formally fixed the boundaries of the settlement. Not long after the American settlement had come formally into being, it merged with the British concession, and thus was the International Settlement born.

“The French Concession was split off from the British concession: after the French merchants had petitioned their own government, and following a year of negotiation, it was formally established in the twenty-ninth year of Daoguang (1849).

“After the Shanghai concessions had been established, the British and French seized upon every sort of pretext to press demands for their extension; and it was thus that the many ‘extra-settlement roads’ of the two concessions came to be built. Our government, though it objected strongly, could do nothing in the matter.

“On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the thirtieth year of the Republic, the Japanese army and navy in China, upon receiving word that Japan's Southern Army had begun its attack on Malaya, at once called on the American and British warships lying at Shanghai to surrender; Japanese troops entered the Shanghai International Settlement and took over the rights and interests of the two nations. The French Concession, though it wished to eke out a little longer, could not in the end have its way.

“The formal recovery of the Shanghai concessions rested upon the new Sino-American and Sino-British treaties of the eleventh of January in the thirty-second year of the Republic, and the new Sino-French treaty of the twenty-eighth of February in the thirty-fifth year. With that, the ‘state within a state’ that had stood at Shanghai for a century vanished utterly.”

From the time Shanghai first had its concessions, strongmen came forth in droves, rising and falling one after another; and after long years of man-made struggle and the winnowing of natural selection, those who at last won mastery numbered but three or four men. Even these few could keep the peace among themselves only where their strength was matched and their interests ran together; once that balance was lost, a fresh round of slaughter would begin.
Zhang Xiaolin was one of these. It is a pity that he had not the least notion of country, still less any grasp of how to move with the changing times—and so he could only meet an unnatural death.

To say, of the Zhang Xiaolin affair, that it was the work of our “Juntong Bureau, Shanghai District” follows as a matter of course and admits of no doubt; for so it is set down alike in the news reports, the commentaries of the day, the work reports, and the archival records. Yet now, more than forty years after the event, were I to say that it was not necessarily the ordinary fruit of some planned deployment on the part of our “Shanghai District,” the thing might well strike people as a novelty. It is not that I would “do the deed and claim no credit,” or cast the glorious sacrifice of my own comrades into the void; it is that, turning over carefully in my mind the whole train of cause and effect and the actual course of the affair, I find in it to this day a great many things that ring false and unreal, to which no firm answer can be had. And so, whether in the end the case was our doing, I am truly of two minds. Or one might put it thus: since the dust has long since settled, and the Zhang case was indeed and in truth our doing, then its success was likewise a thing of chance.

This is by no means a matter of my saying whatever I please; what matters is that it be told just as it was. And because this was a great case, one that left a deeper impression, the things I can remember of it are the more numerous. What follows is the whole warp and weft of the affair—with, to be sure, its tangled and intricate passages here and there.

Before I took over the “Shanghai District”—this was in the twenty-seventh year—the higher authorities had already issued a sanction order against Zhang Xiaolin; and after I took over, in the eighth month of the twenty-eighth year, they restated the earlier order, bidding us find a line to him with all speed and carry out the sanction; and by the twenty-ninth year they were pressing the matter again and again.

To find a lead for the sanction of Zhang Xiaolin, I once called upon Mr. Pan Zixin (see Chapter Five), but with no concrete result. Afterward I went to him twice more, always circling the matter with hints and side-approaches, never finding the chance to raise it head-on; and Mr. Pan, being a man of the keenest, most seasoned shrewdness, took the point at once—only he kept deliberately evading it and would not touch the heart of the matter. It seemed he too had his difficulties, and so I did not pursue it further.

Among the units under the “Shanghai District,” meanwhile, I inquired I know not how many times, and not one of them reported that it had any means to the end. It was only around the sixth or seventh month of the twenty-ninth year that we received a written report from Zhao Sheng (Ji Zhencang), commander of the “Second Action Brigade.” In vague and sketchy terms he said merely that he had already planted an inside line in Zhang's household—mentioning too that the man was one of Zhang's many bodyguards—who set no conditions, needed no support, and would act as opportunity offered. By the rules this report was altogether irregular, for not only did it fail to set out plainly how the man had been approached, won over, and given his task, but—most contrary to all reason—it did not so much as give his name. Having read it, I at once asked Qi Qingbin and Liu Yuanshen to write to Comrade Zhao Sheng of the Second Brigade for an immediate supplementary report. At the time, however, our District headquarters set no strict time limit for a reply, supposing merely that within a few days the particulars would surely come back to us.

Such, in outline, was the internal handling of the case—in fact it was just that simple. Fearing some error, I have gone over it again and again with Yuanshen (then assistant secretary of the “Shanghai District,” in charge of operations, and, besides myself, the only man still living who dealt with this case), and there is no mistake: the Second Brigade's report did indeed give no name for this so-called inside line—not even an alias or a cover name.

At the time we had studied and weighed the Second Brigade's report; and lately, Yuanshen and I have talked the matter over again. Our view is this: between this recruited inside line—or one should rather say this patriot who had undertaken to serve his country—and Zhao Sheng, the Second Brigade's commander, there was no direct link. Very likely several layers lay between them; it may be that Zhao Sheng himself did not know who the man was—this being, too, the care a “middleman” takes to guard security. In an affair of life and death such as this, one cannot secure smooth sailing merely by thumping one's chest and cocking a thumb. Suppose we put it this way: a subordinate of Zhao Sheng's had a friend of a friend, the connection made through one man and then another—so there were several layers already. Everyone, out of goodwill, added a word at each remove, or held a little something back, so that by the time it reached Zhao Sheng it had drifted from the truth of things; and thus what Zhao Sheng reported up to District headquarters could not be full and exact.

On receiving so bare a report, District headquarters had of course to send back for verification; and here, at the start, we may hazard another supposition. Once Zhao Sheng had received the District's instruction to verify, he passed it down again, layer by layer—and never mind whether by word of mouth or in writing—and one cannot know for certain to which layer it reached before, for reasons past guessing, it was suddenly stopped up, so that the reply was long in coming. This interval, reckoned up, was about a month. Just at this juncture someone abruptly shot Zhang Xiaolin dead in his own mansion; and by then the very newspapers had carried the news before the Second Brigade's Zhao Sheng told us that the patriot's name was Lin Huaibu. (In Zhao Sheng's report the last character of the name was at one point miswritten as a homophone.)

At this point one small link must be set down: as to the happening and the spread of this affair, it was in the newspapers that the “Shanghai District” first saw the news, and only afterward received the Second Brigade's report. Until that report came, we were not sure that this was our doing. And another thing: the name the papers carried for the man who did the shooting was “Lin Guifu,” whereas the name in the Second Brigade's report was “Lin Huaibu.” It was a good while later that the public reports settled on “Lin Huaibu” as the patriot's real name.

After the “Shanghai District” received the Second Brigade's report, besides forwarding it up on that basis, we all naturally felt a measure of gladness; and since the thing had succeeded, we duly bade the Second Brigade send up afterward a supplementary report on the whole course of the affair and on Lin Huaibu's personal particulars, for the record. But from the Second Brigade there still came, for a long while, no reply. The news reports of the time ran thus:
The Shanghai Xin Shen Bao of the fifteenth of August, the twenty-ninth year, reported:

“Yesterday at noon a shooting took place within the French Concession of this city. The victim was the Shanghai notable Zhang Xiaolin. Zhang, together with Du Yuesheng and Huang Jinrong, was one of the Three Tycoons of Shanghai, a famed figure of the Green Gang; the names of the three—Huang, Du, and Zhang—were known to almost every woman and child. Zhang was of the ‘Tong’ generation, and so ranked higher than Huang and Du; he was now sixty-eight, a native of Hangzhou, and devoted to the Buddha—there was scarcely a temple hall anywhere but bore a plaque presented by Mr. Zhang. He was violent and coarse by nature, and of late, for all his years, would still fall to reviling people in public. After he had made his name, his every move was far from having Du's discretion and self-restraint, and he had never shaken off the vices of the ‘Shanghai style.’ His residence was on Route Wagner in the French Concession, sharing a single house with Du Yuesheng—Zhang in the eastern wing, Du in the western, with a single courtyard before the house, so that they came and went by the same gate. After the outbreak, Du had gone south to Hong Kong, while Zhang remained living in the house.

“Yesterday afternoon at forty minutes past one, a friend of Zhang's named Wu Jingui came to call, and they fell to chatting upstairs. At that time Zhang's bodyguard Lin Guifu was quarreling with the chauffeur in the courtyard; hearing the noise, Zhang stepped out onto the balcony to rebuke Lin and made to dismiss him from his post. Lin, in a great fury, drew his pistol and fired upward at Zhang, striking him in the head, and he died on the spot.

“After doing the deed, Lin went up the stairs with his pistol and fired at the head of Zhang's friend Wu Jingui, who also took two rounds and expired. The patrolman on guard at the Zhang residence thereupon shut the gate fast, then seized Lin and took him into the police station for examination.

“It is further learned from reliable quarters that after the August Thirteenth Incident Zhang took part in the ‘peace work,’ which drew no little jealousy from the Chongqing side; whether Lin's turning upon his master in this instance was done at Chongqing's instigation is very much a question, and the authorities are giving it close attention.”

The Xin Shen Bao was backed by the Japanese “military authorities,” and so this item ran under the banner headline “City Notable Zhang Xiaolin Shot Dead Yesterday by His Bodyguard,” with a second subhead: “Behind It, Perhaps, Instigation by the Chongqing Puppets.”
Let me first offer a brief gloss on the contents of the item above—

The Green Gang reckoned its lineage by generation. To rank in the “Tong” generation was already to be of the twenty-second remove, which in the Shanghai of that day counted as very high—though not the highest, for above the “Tong” generation there was still the “Da” generation. It was commonly said that Du Yuesheng was of the “Wu” generation, though I cannot vouch for it. In truth, a high generational rank did not necessarily betoken money, power, or standing.

Zhang Xiaolin's being “devoted to the Buddha” did not necessarily mean that he “believed in the Buddha”; this too was a “leaning” common among those who had “laid down the butcher's knife.” A believer, as a rule, keeps the name of Amitabha on his lips—not curses from morning till night.

Again, according to a special dispatch of the Chongqing Ta Kung Pao, filed from Hong Kong at ten in the morning of the fifteenth, with a Shanghai report: “Zhang Xiaolin, at two in the afternoon of the fourteenth, was shot dead at the door of his residence in the French Concession by his bodyguard Lin Guifu. Lin had long served as Zhang's bodyguard at a wage of twenty yuan a month; lately he had asked Zhang for leave and been refused, and Lin said angrily that for twenty yuan a month he could not even have his freedom. Zhang said abruptly that if so, he might hand back his pistol and then do as he pleased. Lin thereupon drew his pistol and fired at Zhang; one round entered by Zhang's mouth and came out at the back of his head, and Zhang fell at once to the ground. Lin then rushed into the room and fired again, killing Zhang. Zhang's protégé Wu Jianchen, a native of Hangzhou, seeing the calamity done, at once telephoned the French police; Lin, seeing this, fired again and shot Wu dead, and as he fled to the gate was seized by the gatekeeper. Zhang held the office of director of the French Concession's Municipal Council, and was sixty-four.”

The same paper, in a special dispatch filed from Hong Kong at eleven at night on the fifteenth, on Japanese authority: “Zhang Xiaolin, killed on the fourteenth, had joined with the Japanese side in forming a ‘Citizens' Association’ and had taken part in the ‘Peace Movement.’ Zhang's protégé Wu Jianchen, shot dead at the same time, was at present ‘director of the Hangzhou Wharf Works Bureau.’”

In this dispatch too the bodyguard who shot Zhang is given as Lin Guifu; as for the name Lin Huaibu, it also appeared in the news—only, more's the pity, no more of the papers of that year can now be found.

The report says Lin's wage was twenty yuan a month—in the fabi then in circulation—and though board and lodging were found for him, this was still, by the general run of Shanghai pay at the time, on the low side. I recall that in our “Shanghai District” the rate for a junior post was forty yuan a month, with board and lodging as well, and for those who took part in outside operations there was an additional operations allowance; and even so most complained of hardship. Set the two side by side, and the gap is wide indeed. It goes to show, too, how meanly Zhang treated those under him.

The Xin Shen Bao gives Zhang's age as sixty-eight; the Ta Kung Pao says sixty-four; while Dacheng magazine has it that on the sixth of the fifth lunar month in the twenty-fifth year of the Republic, Zhang kept his sixtieth birthday—by which reckoning, at his death in the twenty-ninth year, he must have been either sixty-four or sixty-five.

As for the name of the other man killed, the Xin Shen Bao gives Wu Jingui, the Ta Kung Pao Wu Jianchen—each perhaps on some authority of its own, or else the one a name and the other a style. However that may be, the man died wronged.

Zhang Xiaolin held the office of director of the French Concession's council (the papers printed “Gongbuju,” which is wrong: the International Settlement's body was called the Gongbuju, or Municipal Council, and the French Concession's the Gongdongju, or French Municipal Council), and he was besides a “tycoon” of the concessions, so that the French Concession's police authorities kept a resident guard posted at the Zhang mansion. After Lin Huaibu had shot the two men, Zhang and Wu, he meant, one supposes, to force his way out at the gate, and was thereupon seized by the guard on watch there—this being the true state of what the papers called his being “seized by the gatekeeper.”

By all accounts the bodyguards about Zhang were not Lin Huaibu alone; common report put them at a dozen or more, and if not so many as that, then at least a good several. The most baffling thing is that Lin Huaibu alone made any move—one cannot tell where the other bodyguards had got to, or what they were all about.

The same paper, again on “Japanese authority,” had it that “Zhang Xiaolin had joined with the Japanese side in forming a ‘Citizens' Association’ and had taken part in the ‘Peace Movement.’” This may well have been one of the reasons Zhang was sanctioned; but in fact the matter was not so simple. On this point I shall wait and set things out plainly further on.

In the days after the Zhang case, whatever quarter they belonged to, the newspapers of Shanghai, great and small (Shanghai had a great many small papers), did indeed make a clamor of it for a good while; but now, alas, one truly cannot find many of them, and I have only the two items given above.

Next let me set down, in the main, how the “Shanghai District” handled the case. The Second Brigade's Zhao Sheng submitted his report that very night; passed along by courier, it reached me only the next morning—which is to say, I saw the newspapers first and the report after. For in that day there was not only no television, there was not even a wireless set.

By habit I read the paper first thing on rising. That day, opening the paper, I was startled to find the news that Zhang Xiaolin had been shot dead; and reading the particulars more closely, I saw it reported everywhere that his bodyguard, in a fit of anger, had fired up the stairs from below and killed him. Laying the paper down to think, I felt at once the intimation—could this be the Second Brigade's doing?

Ordinarily I would go first to the other offices and only then to the “First Office,” usually sometime after noon. That day, the moment I was out the door I made straight for the “First Office,” anxious to see whether a report had come from the Second Brigade. It too was on Seymour Road, not far from where I lived; and the moment I stepped in I saw that Qingbin and Yuanshen had already laid the Second Brigade's report out before my seat.

The Second Brigade's written report was no more than a short little slip of paper, its gist being that the inside line the Brigade had planted had done its work and completed the task. The time was two in the afternoon of the fourteenth of August, the place Zhang's residence on Route Wagner in the French Concession; the man who carried it out was named Lin Huaibu (first written with one character for “bu” and then altered to another)—only he had been arrested on the spot immediately after, and was straightway taken to the French police station, where interrogation was under way.

Plainly the Second Brigade's report was less detailed than the news; but however detailed the papers might be, for us that did not count, and could serve at most as reference. What we went upon was still the official report.

I decided at once to “forward the matter up as reported,” and wrote back to the Second Brigade, commending them and bidding them contrive with all speed to make secret contact with Lin Huaibu, held at the French police station, so as to gain an understanding of the whole case.

Besides this, I had a mind to use my connection with Maron, the French inspector at the French police station, to protect and look after Lin Huaibu so far as might be. But Qi Qingbin, the District secretary, thought otherwise. In his view, given Maron's place and powers, he might not be able to help; and more, to go this way would not only expose our own intent but leave a trace behind—better to leave the Second Brigade to contrive for itself. I have always respected his judgment, and where the reasoning was sound, all the more did I heed it.

On the afternoon of the fifteenth, we received a telegram from Bureau headquarters at Chongqing inquiring into the shooting of Zhang, with orders to reply the moment it arrived—which shows how closely the higher authorities were following the matter. As luck would have it, our earlier wire had not yet gone out, so we added a few words and sent the whole up together in reply.

Some days later the higher authorities wired a reward of ten thousand yuan, making no close inquiry into the particulars of the case—a sign that they had already acknowledged it as accomplished. On the side of the “Shanghai District,” the writer himself included, no one raised any doubt about the case; and the world outside, of course, took it for a patriotic deed.

Yet the Second Brigade, which had carried out this case, sent up no further report on Lin Huaibu's situation after his arrest. When District headquarters passed the reward on to the Brigade, neither did they, as custom required, report to the District how it had been apportioned, for the record. Hard upon this the Brigade sanctioned the puppet mayor of Shanghai, Fu Xiao'an—a case that made a greater sensation than Zhang's; and since everyone was busy with the Fu case, the Zhang case was set aside for the time.

Recalling it again more closely: the Second Brigade's report gave only the name Lin Huaibu, and of Lin Huaibu's personal particulars said not one word; as for the scene itself, with Lin under arrest there was of course no way to learn of it. Further, the news reports all said that another man, one Wu, had also been shot dead by Lin Huaibu—yet of this there was nothing in the Second Brigade's report.
The above is the course of our handling of the Zhang case; it cannot be said to be without gaps, but in the main this is how it stood.
With that, the sanction of Zhang Xiaolin became a “settled case.”

A note by the writer: the news material quoted above (the Xin Shen Bao clipping and the transcript of the Ta Kung Pao) was sent to me by my friend Pei Kequan, to whom my thanks. The large batch of clippings on the killing of Japanese soldiers in Shanghai, in the previous installment, was likewise supplied by Kequan, and for that too I give thanks.

Pei Kequan served in the twenty-sixth year as a direct-line courier of the “Shanghai District,” and was later transferred to be a colonel-secretary in the political department of the “Loyal and Patriotic Army.” In the thirty-fourth year he was head of an aviation inspection office at Lanzhou. He is now in Taiwan, and publishes writings from time to time.

In the several decades since, no one on the side of the “Juntong Bureau” has ever raised a doubt about the Zhang Xiaolin case. Had I not been writing Shanghai's Behind-the-Lines Operations Against Japan, I too should long since have flung the matter far from me. But lately—around the days just before the Spring Festival of the seventy-third year—as I inquired everywhere after the whereabouts of this man Lin Huaibu, the upshot was that no one, the postwar “Shanghai District” included, knew a thing. I dearly wished to find some old comrade of the former “Second Brigade” and ask, but I do not even know where they have all got to now—whom am I to seek out? Were the former “Second Brigade” commander Zhao Sheng (Ji Zhencang) still living, he ought to be the one who knew the case most deeply and most fully; but he is said not to have got out of the mainland, and whether he is now alive or dead is unknown. Besides him, the writer is the man who “carries on from those above to those below,” and at present I should be the one who knows the most. Even as I put my papers in order I feel the material still not full enough; and turning the whole case over again, most carefully and again and again, I cannot shake the sense that something in it is not quite right. Since there is no way to obtain proof, let me simply set out, one by one, the things my mind has touched upon and sifted, for what they may be worth.

Here I must state one thing plainly: the frame of mind in which I served in the “Shanghai District” in those days, and the frame of mind in which I now write Shanghai's Behind-the-Lines Operations Against Japan, are wholly different. To put it plainly: back then, had anyone said the “Zhang case” was not our doing, I would have “argued it out on the merits”; whereas now the first to harbor doubt is myself—for there are indeed a great many doubtful points in this case. As I have said before, it is not that I turn my hand this way and that and write whatever I please; since I am setting down things past, I must be faithful to the truth, and so I tell it just as it was. Happily it is all long over and done with, and even if the verdict were overturned and it were established that we did not do it—what of it?

Let me begin with the man Lin Huaibu. Who was Lin Huaibu? No one knows. I do not know; Zheng Xiuyuan—once secretary of the “Shanghai District,” afterward chief of the Bureau's personnel department—does not know; Liu Yuanshen, the assistant secretary then in charge of operations in the “Shanghai District,” does not know; the two district chiefs, principal and deputy, of the postwar “Shanghai District” do not know; and the writer, who at the end of the thirty-fourth year again took up the post of “chief of the Third Station, Shanghai District,” does not know either. Truly, this only “Heaven knows.”

As to whether there was a “personnel card” for Lin Huaibu in this District's files, my own judgment is that there would not be; for at the time the “Shanghai District” never sent up Lin's personal particulars at all, so on what would Bureau headquarters have based any “entry”? Still, what I myself know is limited; I have already asked someone to look into it, and when there is a result, I shall add it as a supplementary note when this book is published.

The three characters “Lin Huaibu” did indeed appear in the Shanghai press; the Second Brigade's report plainly wrote “Lin Huaibu”; and the man who killed Zhang Xiaolin was his bodyguard Lin Huaibu—so that the existence of a man called Lin Huaibu is beyond question. But whether his true name and surname were really “Lin Huaibu”—that is another matter. To this very day there is not a shred of firm evidence that he was called “Lin Huaibu.” Where, then, did the name “Lin Huaibu” come from? I do not know. Be that as it may, when I mention his name below, it will naturally still be Lin Huaibu.

After Lin Huaibu had been taken and locked up by the French police, did the Second Brigade have any contact with him at all—a prison visit, say, a little slip of paper with a few words of comfort, a bit of pocket money, a home-cooked dish or two to relieve his cravings? Such are the tokens that feeling and duty require; and given the general social background and connections of the Second Brigade's men, it would by no means have been beyond them—had they wished to do it, I am sure they could have. And if they feared being drawn into the case, they ought at the very least to have gone to comfort Lin Huaibu's family, if only for common humanity's sake. I do not know what, in the end, the Second Brigade did for Lin Huaibu afterward. For this is not merely a question of human feeling; it also tests just what sort of relation there was between the Second Brigade and Lin Huaibu.

When all is said, Lin Huaibu remains, to my mind, a figure of mystery. Bureau headquarters and the “Shanghai District” saw the name Lin Huaibu but once, in the Second Brigade's report; beyond that, no one ever came into contact with the man himself.

Two years or so ago I saw, in a magazine published in Taiwan in April of the sixty-fifth year of the Republic, a piece titled “The Truth of Zhang Xiaolin's Killing,” said to have been written in his own hand by Lin Huaiguo (that is, Huaibu) after he was released from prison at the war's victorious end, under the heading “Why Did I Assassinate the Traitor Zhang Xiaolin?”—and to have been published openly at the time in a Shanghai literary miscellany monthly. The piece caught my attention despite myself; before I had read it, I supposed that Lin Huaibu had really been traced at last, and that it would surely disclose the longed-for “truth.” To my surprise, it was better left unread: the more I read, the more preposterous it grew, until I could conclude that it was, in fact, a “frivolous piece,” and my hopes came to nothing. As for the untruth and unreality of this thing, I shall wait to point them out one by one in the next section, and leave it aside here.

Let me next give again, in brief, the personnel background and social ties of the “Second Action Brigade,” and then bring in the present case. In the first chapter of this book I said, in outline: “The forming of this Brigade had no little history behind it; it is said to have been a collaboration between our Mr. Dai and the Shanghai notable Mr. Du Yuesheng, and a form of support that Mr. Du gave to Mr. Dai. And so the chief cadres of the Brigade were, as a rule, either Mr. Du's ‘students’ or of his ‘following.’” A collaboration of this type was rarely seen in the past; to put it concretely, in point of the substance of the war of resistance against Japan it was of course a close joining of a government organ with a latent force of society, while in other respects—privately, one might say—there was inevitably a mutual making-use of one another as well.

The “students” here spoken of paid homage to a “teacher”; the so-called “following” paid homage to an “old man.” Such things were much in vogue in the Shanghai of old; here and now they are, I fear, no longer much in fashion, though some trace of them lingers still. The Second Brigade's members, from the commander down, were made up of just such elements. What they professed was brotherly loyalty; what they somewhat lacked was political consciousness; and their greatest asset must be counted their advantage of ground.

The “Second Action Brigade” was formally entered into the establishment of the “Shanghai District,” treated on the same footing as the other action brigades, and paid its monthly “living and operations allowance” by the rules; the “Shanghai District” too held absolute command over it, and did not regard it with special favor on account of its peculiar background. Of its earlier course I am not too clear; during my tenure as district chief no personnel trouble ever arose. The Brigade kept a full strength of fifty or sixty men at ordinary times, with latent reserves besides to draw upon when needed. That is to say, they were not, in fact, only this many; those brought onto the Second Brigade's rolls—those entered in the register and drawing pay—were but fifty or sixty. When more manpower was needed to support some task, more could be called up at any time.
Such, in the main, is the situation as I understand it; as for what compact there may have been between Mr. Dai and Mr. Du, that I do not know.

In the two years and more that I was chief of the “Shanghai District,” I met the Brigade's commander, Comrade Ji Zhencang, but once; we were together no more than ten minutes, and exchanged only a few words—no more than that. As for the commander's aides and the other cadre comrades, I never came into contact with a single one; apart from the work relation, one may say, there was no private intercourse between us. And so, naturally, I was fairly in the dark as to the Brigade's inner affairs.

Now let me speak of the Second Brigade's connection with the present case. The “Shanghai District” had a dozen or more action units, great and small, with several hundred men among them; why was it that no other unit could plant an inside lead in Zhang Xiaolin's household, and the Second Brigade alone had the means? This surely had to do with its situation. For the Second Brigade's men all had ties to the Du household, and their coming and going there was of course no difficulty; and the Du family's old residence was on Route Wagner in the French Concession, sharing one gate with Zhang Xiaolin's—so that, in such a case, if one set one's mind to picking out a mark from among Zhang's bodyguards, dropping a word here, promising handsome rewards there, or else by the regular method stirring his patriotic ardor and urging him to a bold stroke against the traitor, none of it would likely have been hard. And this was the Second Brigade's best warrant for being able to report that an inside line had been laid.
This is no more than a fancy of my own, meant only to show how very possible it was for the Second Brigade to plant an inside line in the Zhang household; whether it was so in fact, who can say.

Further on, I must come to the question of “the Zhang case and Mr. Du.” I too am, at bottom, one who asks—but of whom am I to ask? And who is qualified to answer such questions? For now, it were best to offer some odds and ends of material and let each reader judge for himself, according to his own “lights”—would that not be the fairer way?

The rumor abroad that the Zhang case had to do with Mr. Du must be taken in two parts. First: that the government's order to sanction Zhang Xiaolin came of Du's attacking him from behind—or, as it is put, of Mr. Du's ceaselessly egging Mr. Dai on to it. Second: that Zhang's bodyguard killed Zhang Xiaolin because Du had directed his men to do so.

These various sayings cannot all be dismissed as mere “idle talk,” but for the most part they are only conjecture. As to the first: the government's order to sanction Zhang Xiaolin had a gravity of its own, and could by no means be swayed by any personal connection; and as to who made the final decision, the writer has said again and again that our Bureau had no power of decision. As to the second point—that is far too tangled to be made plain in a few words.

The “Second Action Brigade” under the “Shanghai District” was, at bottom, bound up with Mr. Du, as I have shown again and again above. For the “Shanghai District” to assign a task to the Second Brigade was a thing within its authority; and for the Second Brigade to receive its instructions, plant an inside line, and undertake the work of killing the traitor was, of course, no more than its due duty. This is the most ordinary formula of the thing.

But because Mr. Du's private relation with Zhang Xiaolin was out of the common—they had indeed once been “as close as brothers,” as all his following of course knew—one asks: when they were ordered to carry out the sanction of Zhang, might they not have “privately” put the question to Mr. Du? By our own code this was absolutely forbidden; yet the writer dare not say, of the comrades of the Second Brigade, whether in the end they held the discipline of the organization the weightier—or the loyalty owed to a master and his school.

All the world knows that after the war began Du went to Hong Kong and Zhang stayed in Shanghai, and that a rift had opened between the two. To what degree, in the end, they were at odds, I do not know. Might Mr. Du, seizing the occasion of the government's order to sanction Zhang, have “lent encouragement” or “given help” from the side? That is a hard answer to come by; for my part, I truly know nothing of it whatever. And yet—how should I not have wished to know?
Layer upon layer, fold upon fold—there are mysteries here past all sounding.

To come, at this point, back to the main thread: in the report the Second Brigade wrote to the “Shanghai District,” they gave beforehand no name for the inside line, and afterward sent up no supplementary account of how the case had come about. Was there not, in this, some hidden circumstance? Had they held certain facts back—or did they have scruples about speaking them out?

I believe that Comrade Zhao Sheng, the Second Brigade's commander, was always upright, steady, and forthright; and being the man he was, he would never have made a false case out to be true—having in truth no connection with Lin Huaibu at all, and then, after the event, forced himself into it to claim the credit—for the upshot of such a thing would surely be to overreach and undo oneself, even to ruin. If he hid the facts, he must have had his own bitter reasons.
Yet however one puts it, I for my part feel there are a great many doubtful points in the case, and unless each is cleared up and established, it is hard to be convinced. For instance:

That beforehand the name of the inside contact, once he had been arranged, was not reported to the District for the record, as the rules require, was altogether irregular; and if they truly did not know it, that would have to be explained in full and approved by the higher authorities.

Afterward, Lin Huaibu having been arrested, they ought by every means to have contrived to make contact with him—that only stands to reason. How much the Second Brigade did on this head I do not know, for after the instruction went out there was never any word.

After the war's victorious end, it was rumored that Lin Huaibu had been released from prison; but for all my inquiries among the comrades concerned, no one knew anything of it, still less could I find a single person who had known Lin Huaibu. It was rumored that after his release the Bureau had found him a place—but for this too no ground could be found.

The greatest doubt is Lin Huaibu's killing of Zhang Xiaolin: since it came after he had been cursed and abused, was it in truth a flash of the moment's passion—or a situation deliberately contrived after he had received his orders? On this point I have a supposition. Suppose, say, that Lin Huaibu were living now, and one asked him to his face: even were it a simple act of revenge to vent his spleen, he would still say it was rooting out a traitor for his country. Plainly the weight of the two is far, far apart. (These are words that ought not to be written down; I beg your pardon for them.)

There is yet another point past explaining. Lin Huaibu had been in the Zhang household a good while, and was of course thoroughly familiar with his surroundings; can it be that it never occurred to him that he would not get away afterward? Or had he arranged a way out for himself? Might someone have hinted to him: “Go ahead, never mind; if you're taken in, we have the means to get you out”?

There is one matter on which it will not do to keep silence, and which must here be set right; for I have ample grounds to point out, one by one, that it is not true—though not everyone, it may be, can tell the true from the false.

—— Magazine, published in Taipei in April of the sixty-fifth year of the Republic, carried a piece titled “The Truth of Zhang Xiaolin's Killing,” signed Dongguo Ya—a pen name, of course. Before the piece Mr. Dongguo Ya set down a few words, as follows: “Lately I chanced to read, in a certain journal, an account of the inside story of Zhang Xiaolin—that Shanghai man-about-town whose name stood level with Du Yuesheng's and Huang Jinrong's—full of untruths, and laughable. After the war's victorious end, when I was editing a literary miscellany monthly in Shanghai, I received a letter in his own hand from Mr. Lin Huaiguo, the patriot who shot the traitor Zhang (writer's note: the original has ‘guo,’ not ‘bu’), titled ‘Why Did I Assassinate the Traitor Zhang Xiaolin?’ (an open letter to the compatriots of the whole nation), and I published it. I now copy it out and send it to your magazine for republication, to set the record straight and make the truth plain. Dongguo Ya, the fifteenth of the first month.”

First let it be made clear: the man who shot Zhang Xiaolin was named “Lin Huaibu,” not “Lin Huaiguo.” At first I took it for a slip of the pen or a printer's error; but the piece has it “guo” both times it appears, and where the mistake truly lies I cannot tell. Lin Huaibu is one of the principals of this case, and of no small importance; his name, of course, admits of not the slightest error. Writing this, I am suddenly put in mind that when the “Shanghai District” received the “Second Action Brigade's” written report after the event, several of us had our doubts about this character “bu” in Lin Huaibu's name—for a “bu” in a personal name is a very rare thing indeed.

I had not meant to set down the whole text, but feared that to do otherwise would be called quoting out of context; happily the piece is not very long. Besides pointing out the untruths in it, I may by its means answer, too, certain questions of the “one might well ask” sort—and those with no direct bearing on the case I shall simply spare. Here, then, is “The Truth of Zhang Xiaolin's Killing”—which is nothing of the sort—the original as the so-called Lin Huaibu wrote it to Dongguo Ya:

“Dear Editor: When the guns of August the Thirteenth roared out in the twenty-sixth year of the Republic, they stirred in every compatriot the heart to save the nation; and to the song, raised everywhere across the land, of ‘Worker, farmer, soldier, student, merchant—all together save the nation!’ who knows how many hot-blooded youths left their homes of their own will and set out upon the great road of salvation, to win their motherland its survival.

“At that time I too joined the Shanghai cultural circles' national-salvation work-team, led by Mr. Liu Naifu, which was soon merged into the Military Affairs Commission's training regiment,(1) He Xingjian's unit, doing propaganda and the organizing of the populace and the like, active through Shu, He, and Lu and thereabouts in central Anhui, where we won over a great mass of the people. Just as training was beginning, the area was, unexpectedly, made over to the Fifth Route Army to garrison, and the training regiment was ordered to march to Tunxi and be reorganized into the Loyal and Patriotic Army; and I was again transferred to the enemy's rear to take up secret work, returning to Shanghai by way of Hong Kong and Guangdong,(2) whereupon I made contact with Comrade ——— of the Juntong Bureau's Shanghai District action brigade and set to work.(3)

“By then Shanghai had become a Solitary Island, hard pressed by the forces of the enemy and the puppets, and the work was fairly difficult; but my comrades had all been strictly trained and one and all held to a resolve of sacrifice, and though the enemy and the puppets guarded against us by every means, we still made the work our aim, and besides destroying the enemy's military,(4) we sanctioned the shameless traitors who sold out the country.

“When the Reformed Government was set up and the whole rabble came to power, the Shanghai notable Zhang Xiaolin would not heed the counsel of his good friend Du Yuesheng, but instead conspired with the traitors Liang Hongzhi, Chen Qun, and the rest, fawning upon the enemy, going nightly to the Kunshan Garden in Hongkou to confer with the enemy generals Changqi, Matsui, and others,(5) resisting his own country, abetting the enemy's aggression, insulting our Leader, wrecking the resistance, and sending men to Hong Kong to assassinate Du Yuesheng.(6) The government had by then obtained intelligence of it;(7) but, disposed to leniency,(8) it sent men to advise him on the spot and bade him repent and turn over a new leaf. This man, past all sense, would not be moved, and so we made our first attempt at the sanction, at the corner of Avenue Foch and Yates Road;(9) but because his chauffeur was ‘quick-witted’ and, heedless of all, sped through a red light, the blow missed. Then I was sent, using an old personal connection, to enter the Zhang residence(10) and serve as a guard; at first I could not bring myself to kill him, and would often remonstrate with him from the side,(11) hoping he would exert himself for the government and be at once loyal and righteous—but, alas, in his dotage he was besotted with fame and gain, and grew only the worse. By the night of August the Thirteenth in the twenty-ninth year, when he was attending an important meeting of the enemy and the puppets at the Liusan Garden,(12) I meant to seize the chance and take the whole nest of traitors in one sweep; but, as it happened, he took one or two of his intimates with him and had me keep watch at the house, so that once again the sanction came to nothing.(13)

“The next day, August the Fourteenth, I asked leave on a plea of illness, the better to plan again how to deal with him.(14) Not only did he refuse—he suspended me from my post; and I bethought me that to dwell in the tiger's den and yet not take the tiger—when, then, was I to wait for? When he went upstairs and called on me to hand over my pistol, I seized the chance: taking careful measure of the ground, I raised my pistol and fired two rounds up the stairs,(15) and fearing, since I had not seen him, that I might have missed, I hurried up to look—and met at the head of the stairs his follower Wu Hong (director of the puppet paper-goods tax bureau),(16) frozen with terror into a dumb thing; him too I shot dead with a single round, and hastening to the second floor saw that the traitor Zhang had already been shot dead. I judged the task done; but the police had already got wind of it and sent a great body of detectives to surround the Zhang residence, so that I could not get away. Holding fast to a resolve to succeed or die a martyr, I put the pistol to my temple to take my own life—only, as it fell out, my rounds were spent and I failed.(17) I was afterward sentenced to fifteen years, and passed more than five years of bitter life in prison, until, victory being happily won, I recovered my freedom.

“On coming out of prison I found my aged mother blinded by grieving over me, my wife long since living by hired labor, my six- or seven-year-old child unschooled, the whole family worse off than beggars. In my heart I grieved, of course, and yet was glad too, for after all the nation had won its victory, and traitors great and small were being brought to the judgment of the law. But many outside misunderstood me, supposing that I had received a handsome reward from the government. Some even said that I had sanctioned the traitor Zhang at Mr. Du Yuesheng's direction, and that a great sum for my living had been passed to me through Wan Molin—which grieved me the more.(18) I know only that when a nation stands or falls, for the common man to give his life is the mark of a young man's loyalty and faith; to sanction a traitor I did, of course, on orders—that others should suspect me of coveting money and being bought by a private man is nothing less than a slander upon my character.

“As for a government reward, to this day I have not had a single copper; and as for Mr. Du, to this day we have never so much as met face to face. My present work is no more than that of an ordinary investigator in the —— Bureau. Yet I take much comfort in it, for there are still many comrades who suffered and who to this day have no way forward; I hope the authorities will show them a little care, enough to give heart to those who come after.

“Your magazine, in its published aims, avows that it commends unknown writers and champions a free literature; and though I am no writer, I am fond of letters, and so have freely written this letter—unliterary, but true in fact(19)—to declare to my compatriots and comrades, in full, the truth of the matter. Written by the hand of Lin Huaiguo.”

That the patriot Lin Huaibu struck down the Shanghai tycoon Zhang Xiaolin is a fact true beyond all doubt; and whatever his motive, we hold this patriot's brave deed in respect throughout. But as for the letter above, we make bold to conclude that it by no means came from Lin Huaibu's hand—which is to say, it is a forgery under his name. How do we know? By the marks set in the original text, there are eighteen points that may serve to refute it:
(1) There was no training regiment directly under the Military Affairs Commission.
(2) From Tunxi in Anhui province to Shanghai, there was no need to go round by Hong Kong and Guangdong in a great detour. Anyone who traveled this road in wartime knew the way to go.

(3) The writer was the highest officer of the “Shanghai District,” and among its eight action brigades there was never, whether by true name or cover name, any such man as Lin Huaibu (nor any Lin Huaiguo). And even if I could not keep so many names in mind, surely I would have known after the event?

(4) “Destroying the enemy's military”—this is not the sort of phrase a trained man would use; at the least one would have to add after “military” some noun like “installations” or “plans” to make a proper term of it.

(5) That Zhang Xiaolin went nightly to Hongkou to confer with the enemy generals “Changqi,” “Matsui,” and the rest—this, first of all, I do not believe, for Zhang Xiaolin was not of that stuff, still less of that standing. I do not know who among the Japanese commanders “Changqi” or “Matsui” might be; but I do know that there are Japanese surnamed Nagasaki—and none surnamed Changqi.
(6) That Zhang Xiaolin sent men to Hong Kong to assassinate Du Yuesheng—this is news; not that such a thing could never be, but what we would ask is: whence did this “author” come to know it?
(7) “The government had by then obtained intelligence”—that the government should obtain intelligence is within his knowledge too; how vast, then, are his magic powers?
(8) If Zhang did send men to assassinate Du and failed, the one disposed to be lenient and to think no thought of revenge should be Du—not the government.

(9) The “we” here spoken of should be the “Shanghai District action brigade”; yet of this “first attempt at the sanction (of Zhang Xiaolin), at the corner of Avenue Foch and Yates Road,” the writer, as chief of the “Shanghai District,” knew nothing at all.

In the book Bygone Days in Shanghai there is likewise a passage that runs: “Our own action men still found a way to catch him off his guard. By prior arrangement, one night, when the motorcade of Marshal Zhang (meaning Zhang Xiaolin) reached the crossing of Shanzhong Road and Avenue Joffre, the light suddenly turned red, and the Marshal's motorcade had to brake and stop. In that very instant the action men lying in wait at the street corner opened a furious fire with a submachine gun. The Marshal's driver, Ah Si, who doubled as the head of his bodyguards, was very quick; the moment the shots rang out he stamped hard on the accelerator and ran the red light. And so, by a hair's breadth, he saved the Marshal's life.”

Now, Bygone Days in Shanghai was published in the sixth month of the sixty-second year, whereas this “Truth of Zhang Xiaolin's Killing” is marked by its author as sent to —— Magazine in the first month of the sixty-fifth year—the one earlier, the other later; yet the incidents in the two tales are cut from the same cloth, only the place of the mishap differs. To put it bluntly, the latter is rather open to the suspicion of having “drawn its material” from the former.

This, of course, is not enough to serve as proof; but the writer will say further, and with assurance—whether the thing happened at “the crossing of Avenue Foch and Yates Road” or at “the crossing of Shanzhong Road and Avenue Joffre,” there was no such affair at all; for at bottom our “Shanghai District” had no “submachine gun.” Asked about it, the former district secretary Zheng Xiuyuan had likewise heard nothing of it.

(10) None of the action units under the “Shanghai District” had been able to send a man into the Zhang residence to serve as a guard. Such a thing would have been more than one could ask for; had it happened, it would surely have been reported.

(11) If one had got inside the Zhang residence, the very aim was to sanction Zhang Xiaolin—where, then, is the sense of “could not bring himself to kill him”? And as for “would often remonstrate with him from the side,” that is more preposterous still.
(12) In what capacity, by what standing, Zhang Xiaolin is supposed to have attended an important meeting of the enemy and the puppets, one cannot tell.

(13) I would ask this “gentleman”: if Zhang Xiaolin had reckoned you an intimate and taken you along to the meeting, could you, single-handed and alone, have swept up the whole nest of traitors in one net? And then, what of those Japanese—where would you have put them?

(14) A man truly trained in secret-service work and charged with an action task ought to have known that “asking leave on a plea of illness” had already broken a great taboo; and that he should still plan to go out and “plan how to deal with him”—one cannot tell what he meant to plan.

(15) Had Zhang not suspended you from your post, would you never have bethought yourself of why you had entered the tiger's den at all? If, on the other hand, one says that Zhang Xiaolin not only refused you leave but bade you hand over your pistol, dismissed you from your post, and abused you into the bargain, thereby rousing you to fury and at the same time firing your courage, so that you shot him—that would be more in keeping with reason.

(16) The other man shot is given by the papers now as “Wu Jingui,” now as “Wu Jianchen,” and here again as “Wu Hong.” His office is called now “director of the Hangzhou Wharf Works Bureau,” now “director of the Jiangsu provincial tinfoil tax bureau,” and here it is noted as “director of the puppet paper-goods tax bureau.” What, in the end, was his name? What did he do? To learn that, one would have to go and verify it all over again.

(17) By this piece's own account, he “fired two rounds” at Zhang Xiaolin and “one round” at the man Wu—three rounds discharged in all—so that when he came to put the pistol to his temple to kill himself, his “rounds were spent.” I would ask: were there really but three rounds loaded in the pistol? Did Lin himself not know how many rounds his own pistol held?

(18) True, there is indeed such a rumor abroad; but as to whether Mr. Du had anything to do with the Zhang case, the writer of course cannot know, and I believe no one now living knows either. As for talk that chases the wind and clutches at shadows, out of mere surmise—how can that be reckoned to count?

(19) This “Truth of Zhang Xiaolin's Killing,” by the account of the one signing himself Dongguo Ya, was published in Shanghai after the war's victorious end; but with neither the name of the journal nor the date of publication given, who is to know whether it is true or false? On one point, though, some corroboration is possible: in those years—that is, between the thirty-fourth and the thirty-eighth—a man who had carried out action work, and was besides a serving investigator in the —— Bureau, would absolutely not have been permitted to publish the particulars of a case, and the Zhang case would be no exception. However fond of letters he might be, he could not take such a thing for his subject-matter. That he should now, of all things, publish “an open letter to the compatriots of the whole nation” is truly beyond all imagining.

These nineteen points above are the writer's own view of this “Truth of Zhang Xiaolin's Killing”—nothing more than taking the matter on its merits, with no meaning beyond it. In sum, this thing is a patchwork cobbled together, with no complete foundation in fact; it gets wrong even the name of one of the case's principal figures, let alone the rest.
After the piece there is a long passage of “Dongguo Ya's comment” besides, which I shall not dwell upon here.

The sanction, in action work, of a particular target may, in the advanced nations of the future, become a relic of history. Yet in certain backward countries in a period of transition, it will still persist, in some altered form.

That we did such things in those days was brought about by extraordinary circumstances and sudden events; there was in truth no choice. Hereafter, when men and times and places and things are all no longer what they were, there will be, I believe, all too many reasons why such things will not often occur; and the most conspicuous of them is that such extreme measures are, in the end, not quite in accord with the common feeling of mankind.

As for individuals, our comrades were none of them fond of killing; that it could hardly be avoided was because we were “at war.” Everyone understands that in war men die. But to kill too many is not only no fine thing to boast of; it leaves, besides, many a burden on the mind that one cannot lay down. Asked how it feels, one may truly say there is a taste of it in the heart all its own.

The case in which the patriot Zhu Sheng cleft Fu Xiao'an with an axe must be counted the most forceful action of all; the dead man received his deserved punishment, and we, for the sake of the resistance's future, did our duty as well.

This case has a great distinction, and a rare one: consider that the patriot Zhu was a common man of the people, who had not joined our organization nor undergone any strict training, and yet dared to swing the axe and strike—can such courage be roused by money alone? And so we would point out: a traitor is one whom any man may put to death, and it is men of Fu Xiao'an's kind who deserve to be called traitors of the standard sort.

From the end of the twenty-ninth year into the beginning of the thirtieth, just as the Wang puppets were bent upon getting up their puppet regime, they did—Zhou Fohai the prime mover, with Li Shiqun and the rest lending their aid to the tyrant—a great many wicked things to the nation's hurt. One was the taking over of our government's “Special District Court” within the Shanghai concessions; another was the setting up of the bogus “Central Reserve Bank,” to wreck the existing currency system and strike at the government's financial policy.

Against these two things, besides submitting detailed material, the “Shanghai District” was also ordered to contrive to check them, or to throw them into disorder; and so another struggle unfolded. The most execrable thing of all was that the fanatics of the Wang puppets went so far as to take a bloody revenge, and thereby harmed some scores of innocent people besides.
